symptoms.name: Masking until you're exhausted

clips.title: AuDHD explained: Can you have ADHD and autism at the same time?
clips.text: Masking behaviors are an important thing to look out for with both ADHD and autism because everybody wants to fit in and show that they're feeling on top of things and successful in life and with either autism or ADHD. This can lead to behaviors like. Really almost pretending to be on top of things at work without asking for help or being exhausted and overwhelmed and not reaching out to people around you. In the end, the more important thing to keep an eye out for is that this often leads to a sense of exhaustion or burnout, or not being authentic to yourself. The bottom line to be looking out for when it comes to that feeling of masking or not being true to yourself is really checking in and making sure that you're feeling a sense of wellbeing and not overwhelmed in life.

symptoms.desc: Masking (camouflaging) is consciously or unconsciously hiding autistic/ADHD traits to appear "normal" — suppressing stims, scripting responses, forcing eye contact. It works socially but costs enormous energy, which is why AuDHD people often crash after social events.

symptoms.name: Difficulty with transitions
symptoms.desc: Task-switching (transitioning) draws heavily on executive function, which is often delayed in ADHD. Moving from one activity to another — especially away from something absorbing — can feel physically hard and needs explicit support rather than willpower.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD

symptoms.name: Interrupting because you'll forget
symptoms.desc: Interrupting to say something before it escapes is a working-memory impulse: in ADHD, holding a thought while waiting for a turn is unreliable, so the brain blurts it out to preserve it. It is usually not rudeness — it is memory management.

symptoms.name: Flat affect (resting face)
symptoms.desc: Flat affect (a neutral resting face) does not mean feeling nothing. In autism, expressive communication differs — the face may not track internal emotion, leading to "resting serious face" and others misreading mood. The feeling is usually much bigger than the face shows.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD

symptoms.name: Fidgeting constantly
symptoms.desc: Fidgeting is automatic movement — tapping, leg-bouncing, pen-clicking — that helps the ADHD/autistic brain maintain arousal and focus. For many it is not a distraction but a regulation tool that actually improves attention.

symptoms.name: Forgetting to eat or drink
symptoms.desc: Forgetting to eat is linked to interoception — sensing internal body signals like hunger — which is often weaker in autism and ADHD, and to hyperfocus that blocks the signal. You can go hours without noticing you are hungry or thirsty.

symptoms.name: Reading social cues wrong

clips.title: 5 Signs You Have AuDHD (ADHD and Autism)
clips.text: Or, you're zoning out because you're overwhelmed and shutting down, or interrupting  because you want to say what you want to say and  ADHD impulsivity pushes you to get it out there. And mix in the autistic tendency not to get social cues exactly right for knowing when to jump in, and before you know it, you've interrupted for the fifth time. And what can you do? Well, if you're like me, the  only way to go, is forward.

symptoms.desc: Reading social cues involves interpreting tone, facial expression, and implied meaning, which autistic social communication processes differently. The result is missed or misread signals — not a lack of care, just a different social operating system.

symptoms.name: Oversharing / too blunt
symptoms.desc: Oversharing or being blunt comes from autistic communication style (direct, literal, honest) and ADHD impulsivity (words out before the filter). It is typically not about attention-seeking — it is treating honesty as the default.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD

symptoms.name: Can't start a task unless it's urgent
symptoms.desc: ADHD motivation is interest- and urgency-based: without a deadline or adrenaline, starting can feel impossible, so last-minute pressure becomes the engine. This 'procrastination' is actually executive function differences, not a character flaw.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD

symptoms.name: Echolalia / repeating phrases
symptoms.desc: Echolalia is repeating words or phrases — often from a show, song, or someone else — as a form of stimming, regulation, or processing. In AuDHD it can be automatic verbal playback used to self-soothe or to hold onto a satisfying sound.

symptoms.name: Sensory-seeking (crash, squeeze, weighted)
symptoms.desc: Sensory seeking is deliberately pursuing input — crashing into cushions, firm hugs, weighted blankets, deep pressure — to balance the nervous system. It is the opposite pole to sensory overload and helps many AuDHD people regulate.

symptoms.name: Invisible panic before phone calls
symptoms.desc: Phone-call anxiety is a common AuDHD freeze: the call is unstructured, with no visible cues and real-time demands on social scripts and attention. The panic — racing thoughts, rehearsing lines, avoiding dialling — is anticipation of an unpredictable social task, not shyness.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD

symptoms.name: Collecting hobbies, finishing none
symptoms.desc: Starting many hobbies and finishing few is the AuDHD pattern of dopamine-driven novelty: the chase of a new interest is rewarding, while follow-through needs sustained executive function. The collection of half-finished projects is the natural result.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD

symptoms.name: Body feels things others don't notice
symptoms.desc: Heightened sensory awareness (hyper-sensitivity) means noticing — and being bothered by — sounds, lights, textures, and body sensations others filter out. Autistic and ADHD nervous systems often lack the usual sensory 'volume control'.

sources.title: Child Mind Institute: Sensory Processing Issues

symptoms.name: Hyperfocus for hours
symptoms.desc: Hyperfocus is an intense state where attention locks onto one thing for hours and the rest of the world — time, hunger, people — drops away. It is the flip side of ADHD inattention: involuntary, powerful, and hard to interrupt.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD
CHADD: Managing Time Blindness at Work

symptoms.name: Scripting what to say
symptoms.desc: Social scripting is preparing exact words for expected situations — greetings, calls, small talk — a common autism masking strategy. It reduces the unpredictability of interaction but consumes working memory and can fail when the conversation goes off-script.

symptoms.name: Detail blindness then whole checklist matters
symptoms.desc: Detail processing differs in AuDHD: autistic attention can lock onto specific details while the bigger picture blurs, and ADHD can skip details that feel uninteresting. Either way, rules, checklists, and order often act as the missing scaffolding.

symptoms.name: Forgot why you walked into the room
symptoms.desc: Walking into a room and forgetting why is working-memory loss in action — the goal thought was displaced by new input (the doorway, the room). It is common in ADHD and described as the brain's RAM being cleared by a context switch.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD

symptoms.name: Textures / tags unbearable
symptoms.desc: Texture and clothing-tag sensitivity is sensory hyper-sensitivity: fabric, seams, and tags generate input that the nervous system flags as genuinely uncomfortable. It is a real sensory difference, not fussiness, and can dominate attention until removed.

symptoms.name: Needs a routine but can't keep one
symptoms.desc: Autistic brains often thrive on predictability and routine, while ADHD brains struggle to initiate and sustain them — the AuDHD contradiction of craving structure and rebelling against it. The result is elaborate planning systems that last days.

symptoms.name: Obsessive rules fairness
symptoms.desc: Strong fairness and rule sensitivity comes from autistic black-and-white thinking and justice sensitivity — a visceral reaction to unfairness or rule-breaking. It reflects a deeply principled, literal relationship with how things 'should' work.

symptoms.name: Can't filter background noise

clips.title: 5 Signs You Have AuDHD (ADHD and Autism)
clips.text: Maybe you're going to a new coffee shop to get work done with a colleague. Seems like a great idea, right? A nice cafe, a little background noise, and productivity mode ON. ADHD loves the stimulation. New environment, people-watching,  something different. So you get there, and for the  first few minutes, it's great. Then suddenly it's all too much.

symptoms.desc: Difficulty filtering background noise is auditory hyper-sensitivity plus ADHD attention: every sound competes for the same attention channel. Cafes and open offices become exhausting because the brain cannot mute the irrelevant sounds.

symptoms.name: Meltdown after masking all day

clips.title: 5 Signs You Have AuDHD (ADHD and Autism)
clips.text: Did I order nachos? Nope. No distractions for autistic brain. It's already halfway into shutdown mode, regretting every life choice  that led to this moment. So you can't focus, you can't  relax, and you're caught in a battle between "let's keep it going" and "if I don't leave immediately I might explode."

clips.title: 5 Signs You Have AuDHD (ADHD and Autism)
clips.text: And for me, ADHD tends to be louder. So it convinces me to go do that thing, to keep going, keep pushing through, until my autistic brain hits  a full meltdown or shutdown because I've ignored my limits for too long. And then it's a complete and  fairly horrible experience when the autistic brain really pushes back. Sometimes where I'm in bed for hours, or even days, because I am so exhausted.

clips.title: Autism vs ADHD: 5 Key Differences Explained
clips.text: Your emotions or stress build  up quietly in the background until it gets too much, then, Boom! out comes the meltdown or shutdown. At least that's how it can look to an observer. As an autistic person, I  might feel the build inside, but not really know what to do with it either, so that's why in point number 1 I said both brains ruminate.

symptoms.desc: An after-masking meltdown is the overflow of a day spent suppressing stims, scripting, and performing 'normal'. Masking depletes the nervous system's regulation budget, and at home — where it is safe — the pressure finally releases.

symptoms.name: Music strictly one song on repeat
symptoms.desc: Playing one song on repeat is a form of stimming and dopamine regulation: predictable, satisfying auditory input that helps focus or soothe. The repetition is calming precisely because it is known and controllable.

symptoms.name: Loves a good spreadsheet to organise

clips.title: 5 Signs You Have AuDHD (ADHD and Autism)
clips.text: Number 1 You create a million tasks and then get paralyzed by the overwhelm. Today's your day to get organized. You sit down, make a beautiful to-do list, maybe even color code it. Add a few sticky notes, or dozens of sticky notes, and while you're at it you'll just jot down a few other projects you've  been meaning to get to.

symptoms.desc: Loving spreadsheets, lists, and colour-coded systems is externalised executive function — offloading the planning and remembering that ADHD brains find unreliable onto a visible structure. The system is the coping mechanism, not the obsession.

symptoms.name: Takes jokes literally
symptoms.desc: Taking jokes literally is about literal, detail-focused language processing common in autism: sarcasm, irony, and implied meaning are decoded as facts. It is not missing humour — the humour is often enjoyed once the intended layer is made explicit.

symptoms.name: Exhausted by socialising even when fun

clips.title: 5 Signs You Have AuDHD (ADHD and Autism)
clips.text: You get the urge to be around people. You make plans, and for the  first 20 minutes, it's fun. And then, your social battery drains instantly. The irony? Sometimes it's actually you, your idea, your setup, your plans. In one of those moments of ADHD impulsivity. So you might even be in your  house with these friends, but now they're all here in your space and you need to hide.

symptoms.desc: Socialising drains AuDHD energy fast because it taxes attention, sensory filtering, scripting, and masking at once — even when it is enjoyable. This is the 'social battery' draining at double speed, which is why after a great night you may crash completely.

symptoms.name: Keeps 'nice to haves' in your bag for 3 months
symptoms.desc: Carrying 'just in case' items for months is planning for every possible future — an anxious, future-thinking habit common in AuDHD (the bag becomes a safety net against being caught unprepared). Forgetting to remove them is the working-memory half.

sources.title: Autism Society: Recognising Autism and ADHD

symptoms.name: Double empathy — reads animals better than people
symptoms.desc: The double empathy problem describes mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic people — neither instinctively reads the other. Many AuDHD people find animal communication easier to read than human social cues, because it is honest and non-verbal.
